courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue: a sequence number per cell
md: Vyukov is explicit: the queue is "not lockfree in the official meaning, just implemented by means of atomic RMW operations w/o mutexes" (RMW is read-modify-write: an instruction such as CAS or fetch-add that reads and writes a location in one indivisible step) and classifies it as having blocking producers and consumers. It is still excellent in practice; just do not cite it as a lock-free progress guarantee.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
md: The misconception that costs the most: that a template id is a stable name for a logging statement. It is a name for a *cluster*, and clusters split, merge, get wildcarded and get evicted. Anything long-lived (a dashboard, an alert rule, a trained model) must key on persisted template text plus an explicit supersedes relation, not on whatever integer the miner handed out last Tuesday.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: MITRE ATT&CK as a coverage map
md: A green cell is not protection. One rule tagged with a technique usually catches one or two of the many ways to perform it. Count a technique as covered only if a test of a realistic procedure produced an alert (lesson 17), and record which procedures were tested.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Do not confuse the two knobs. PI rescales *positions* (every pair by the same $1/s$). NTK-aware changes the *base* (each pair by a different amount). Both leave the model architecture unchanged; only the precomputed cos and sin tables differ.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
md: Overlap condition: $c \ge F/B$. Fast links (NVLink, the TPU inter-chip interconnect or ICI) need blocks of about 1K tokens; slow links need tens of thousands. Causal masks require striping or zigzag chunk assignment, or the busiest rank sets the pace.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
md: A loop is an algorithm's inner step. With enough iterations, a fixed-size block can resolve chains of references, simulate a small computer, or stand in for chain-of-thought steps, without adding parameters. How well *training* finds such a step is a separate, empirical question.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Learned depth per token: Mixture-of-Recursions, Ouro, HRM and TRM
md: Do not compare TRM's ARC numbers with LLM results as if they were the same kind of system. TRM is trained per task family on about 1000 augmented examples with a fixed answer grid; an LLM is a general text model. An independent ARC Prize analysis cited by the TRM paper found deep supervision drove most of HRM's gain (19% to 39%), while the two-level recursion added little (35.7% to 39.0%).

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
md: Hu et al.'s footnote already warned that a small rank should not be expected to work for every task: if the target were a different language than pretraining, full fine-tuning (like LoRA with r equal to the model width) could win. Low intrinsic rank was measured on tasks that are close to what the model already knows.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
md: Near-chance accuracy on a multiple-choice proxy shows the model no longer *answers* those questions. It does not show the knowledge is gone from the weights. The WMDP authors say so themselves: because RMU edits only three layers it "perhaps obfuscates knowledge more than unlearns it", and in their appendix fine-tuning on the forget corpus recovered the performance.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: How a Mac defends itself: the layers from boot to app
md: "Macs don't get viruses" is a myth defenders still meet. Information stealers such as Atomic Stealer (lesson 16) have been sold to criminals as a monthly service since 2023, and Microsoft documented new campaigns delivering them to Macs in 2026. The built-in controls are strong, but they mostly decide what may *launch*; social engineering goes around them.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Unified logging: reading what the Mac recorded
md: Do not expect an attacker's password prompt, curl URL or file path to show up in plain text in the unified log. Default privacy redaction hides many dynamic strings. Plan on Endpoint Security or EDR telemetry for process command lines, and use the unified log for subsystem state changes.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: NIST notes that most samples blend several categories, so the classic labels are 'considerably less useful than they used to be' for incident handling. Use the labels to communicate quickly; spend your time on behaviour and detection.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviours as indicators: persistence, credentials, ransomware
md: Every behaviour rule has false positives: per-user installers for chat and sync clients legitimately write Run keys from AppData. Sigma's falsepositives field is not decoration; tune with an allowlist of known-good signed programs and review what fires.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Truncation does not make the encoder cheaper. Sentence Transformers' docs stress that a Matryoshka model is not faster or smaller to run. What gets cheaper is everything after encoding: storing, indexing and comparing the vectors.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Measuring the result: MFU, HFU and what the numbers count
md: Every knob in this course trades three things: memory per GPU, communication on a specific link, and idle or redundant compute. MFU is the single number that tells you whether the trade worked.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: VADs and malfind: finding code that has no file
md: A clean malfind proves little too. Code injected into an EXECUTE_READ region with a properly mapped file, or code that hides its pages while sleeping (lesson 12), will not match these rules. Use malfind with the other views, never alone.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
md: Internal fragmentation is waste inside handed-out blocks (a rounding cost). External fragmentation is free memory split into holes too small to use (a placement and lifetime cost). Both are measured against live data, and the number depends on when you measure.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: There is no "acquire store" or "release load". Release only affects stores and Acquire only affects loads; SeqCst cannot create them either. A Release store and a Release store never synchronize with each other.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: EBR pays per operation, not per node, and needs no per-node announcement. In exchange, a single thread stalled while pinned blocks all reclamation, so garbage is unbounded.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: The call stack: frames, return addresses and saved frame pointers
md: The stack grows toward lower addresses, so people often assume an overflowing array also spills downward. It does not. `strcpy`, `gets` and loops write from `buf[0]` toward `buf[7]` and beyond, which means toward *higher* addresses: straight into the saved frame pointer and the return address of the same frame.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
md: Re-ID is open-set retrieval: open-set means the people at test time are not among the training classes. You do not predict a label; you learn distances that rank true matches first for people the model has never seen.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
md: Misconception: "warm-up makes a benchmark more accurate". It makes it measure **steady state**. If your function really runs once per request on cold caches, the warmed number is precise and wrong. Decide which regime production is in, then measure that one.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Launching and watching a Miles run
md: Architecture flags are not self-validating. Two checkpoints of one family can ship a different `--rotary-base`, vocab padding or norm epsilon. Diff the checkpoint's `config.json` against its file in `scripts/models/` before a first run and append any drifted value, for example `--extra-args "--rotary-base 10000"`.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
md: The Miles fault-tolerance page is marked **outdated**: it describes the pre-refactor stack, and new machinery is still being merged. Also note that P2P writes are bounded by `--p2p-transfer-timeout` (default 30 s) and a failed write fails the update; the docs state there is no automatic retry or fallback to broadcast.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Before trusting a learned policy, write down what happens when the model is completely wrong. If the answer is "still correct and no worse than a classic algorithm by a bounded factor", you can ship it and let the model only add upside.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Android IPC: exported components, intent redirection, PendingIntents
md: Misconception: "we never exported that activity, so it is not exported." Libraries add components to the merged manifest at build time. Review the manifest of the APK you ship (lesson 3), not the one in your repository.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: Cache size per token is set by what you store per token per layer. MQA and GQA shrink it by sharing keys and values across heads. MLA's bet is different: store one small learned vector per token and let each head derive its own keys and values from it.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs
md: LoRA fine-tunes share a frozen base. A server that keeps the base once and batches requests for different adapters together gets both the memory saving and the batching efficiency that separate deployments throw away.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Many GPUs, many tenants: placement, cold starts and fairness
md: At cluster scale, multi-LoRA serving is a placement problem: consolidate load (Punica), switch merged and unmerged as traffic skews (dLoRA), hide adapter loads (prefetch, async or CPU-assisted prefill), and schedule for fairness across tenants, not only for throughput.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
md: This argument explains the *direction* of a single step, with moving averages switched off. It says nothing about momentum: Bernstein and Newhouse treat the averages as smoothing against mini-batch noise, and call their exact role an open question. Muon adds momentum for empirical reasons.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: An optimizer claim is only as good as its baseline. Ask: was the baseline tuned as hard, at more than one scale and data ratio, compared at the end of training, and in which unit (steps, tokens, FLOPs or hours)? Independent tests put matrix optimizers ahead of AdamW, by less than first reported.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
md: One rule generates muP: every weight and every update should have spectral norm about the square root of fan_out over fan_in. For Adam that means learning rate 1/fan_in for every layer; for SGD, fan_out/fan_in.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: Atomic does not mean cheap. An atomic write to a line that other cores are reading forces cache-line transfers, and in Bos's measurement it made another core's plain loads about 10 times slower on an older x86-64 machine.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC trades space for concurrency: every update leaves an old version behind so that readers already in flight can keep a consistent view without blocking writers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
md: MVCC moves the cost of concurrency into the storage engine: dead versions to clean, index entries to maintain, and XIDs to freeze. Long-lived snapshots make all three worse.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Why states hack: five purposes behind state operations
md: Ask what the operation is *for* before asking who did it. Espionage, disruption, influence, pre-positioning and revenue each predict different targets, dwell times and signs of success, and so different defences.

courseTitle: Nation-state cyber operations and cyber conflict
lessonTitle: Wartime cyber in Ukraine, 2022: wipers, a satellite network, the grid
md: A coincidence in time is not proof of coordination. Mandiant noted the overlap with missile strikes and explicitly declined to claim a link. When you build a timeline, keep "happened at the same time" and "was planned together" as separate statements, with separate evidence.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens
md: Neither NSA nor DSA shrinks the KV cache. NSA adds compressed and per-branch keys; DSA adds an indexer key per token. Both cut the bytes *read and computed* per query. Also, DSA's indexer is still $O(L^2)$ over a sequence, just with a much smaller constant.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Choose by the edits you must survive. Resizes, recompression and tone changes: a perceptual hash with Hamming search is cheap and exact. Crops, overlays, rotations and composites: a learned copy descriptor with nearest neighbor search. Either way, tune the threshold on labeled pairs from your own traffic.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: ARP spoofing up close, and how switches stop it
md: Static ARP entries on every laptop are not a practical fix: they break when hardware changes and do not scale. Put the check in the switch (DHCP snooping plus DAI), where one configuration covers every port, and encrypt traffic so a successful poisoner learns little.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Firewalls: stateless, stateful and application-aware
md: A firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Firewalls decide who may talk to whom on which port; whether the conversation itself is malicious is the job of the application, TLS, and IDS or application-layer inspection.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Suricata in depth: how rules match, EVE output and tuning
md: Every Suricata alert should send you to the flow behind it: pull the EVE records with the same flow_id (or the Zeek logs with the same Community ID) and decide from the full conversation, not from the alert message alone.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Network forensics for incident response: a worked IcedID investigation
md: Network forensics is pivoting with discipline: logs to scope, packets to prove, one UTC timeline, every step recorded. The attacker controls the infected host; they rarely control your sensor.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: UDP and ICMP: no handshake, and messages about the network
md: "Block all ICMP" is a common overreaction. It hides hosts from ping sweeps, but it also breaks useful signals such as fragmentation needed (type 3, code 4), which hosts rely on to size their packets. Filter selectively: allow the error messages your network needs, rate-limit echo, and log the rest.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Setting a policy does not move pages that already exist. `mbind(2)` affects only new allocations unless you pass the flag `MPOL_MF_MOVE` (or `MPOL_MF_MOVE_ALL`, which also moves pages that other processes share, and so needs CAP_SYS_NICE, a Linux capability: one of the slices of root privilege a process can hold). Install the policy before the first touch, or ask for migration explicitly.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
md: NVMe queue depth does not make flash faster; it lets the controller keep many dies busy. One synchronous 4 KB read at a time pays the full read latency per request no matter how many queues the drive has. Use async I/O (io_uring, the Linux asynchronous I/O interface built on shared submission and completion rings; SPDK, or many threads) to keep enough requests in flight.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: A density map gives a number, not a list of objects. You cannot crop, identify or follow an individual from it, and the count is real-valued. Use it when objects are too dense to box, not as a default.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
md: A common misconception: "we log everything, so we are observable". Logs scale with traffic times fields per event, metrics scale with the number of distinct label combinations, and traces scale with the sampling rate. Choosing where each fact lives is the design work.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: A common bug: cropping a single field, such as a price, and running Tesseract with the default `--psm 3`. Automatic page segmentation expects a page and can find no lines at all in a tight crop. Use `--psm 7` (one line) or `--psm 8` (one word), and leave a small white border around the text.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
md: ANLS cannot tell a harmless typo from a costly one: `42.50` predicted as `42.5` scores 0.8, the same as many genuine digit errors of similar size. For money and IDs, add field-level exact match after normalization.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: chroot is not a boundary, and Leaky Vessels shows why
md: chroot changes how paths are looked up, nothing more. Open file descriptors, the working directory and root's privileges all ignore it. Real filesystem isolation needs a mount namespace, no privilege to undo it, and no handles that point outside.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Requirements and collection plans: decide before you search
md: No requirement, no collection. A plan that names sources, legal basis and retention keeps an investigation focused, defensible and small.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Geolocation: finding where a picture was taken
md: Geolocate places and events, not private people. Working out where a private individual lives or goes from their photos is stalking, whatever the technique is called. Practise on public landmarks, games built for it, or published case studies.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Putting it together: an ethical OSINT review, and where to practise
md: Never practise on real private people, including friends who "don't mind". Use public landmarks, fictional scenarios, practice platforms, and your own organisation with written permission.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: A green local run does not prove CI will pass. CI tests your change merged into the latest base branch, on a clean machine, often across several OS and Python versions. Read the workflow file to see what will actually run.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Approve when the change makes the codebase better than it was, not when it matches what you would have written. There is no perfect code, only better code. The goal is continuous improvement.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: A repository with no `CONTRIBUTING.md` in its file list may still have one. It can be in `.github/` or `docs/`, or inherited from the organization's `.github` repository, which never shows up in the repository's own files or clone. Use the link GitHub shows on the new issue or PR page.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Fetch from `upstream`, push to `origin`. Remote-tracking branches like `upstream/main` are snapshots from your last fetch, not live views.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: `-s` adds a Signed-off-by trailer whose meaning the project defines (often the DCO). Read CONTRIBUTING to learn whether the project wants sign-offs, fixups squashed, and which merge method it uses.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: A sign-off you add without reading the DCO is still a legal statement about provenance. Copying code you cannot trace (a gist without a license, generated output in a project that bans it) and signing off is exactly what the DCO exists to prevent.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Regression checks: perf bots and noise thresholds from history
md: Regression checks only work if noise is known. A bot learns each benchmark's normal spread from history and flags changes beyond it; you do the same by hand with repeated, interleaved runs and a test.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: "Same problem" means the *same* failure, not just any failure. If removing a line turns a `StatisticsError` into a `NameError`, you did not shrink the bug; you created a new one. Compare the exception type and message every time, not just whether something crashed.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: Misconception: "small" means "tiny". Google's guide also says a change can be too small to understand: if you add a new API, include a use of it in the same change so reviewers can judge it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: The block table is the whole trick: contiguous logical blocks, scattered physical blocks, allocation on demand. Waste is capped at one partly filled block per sequence.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Prefill on top of a cached prefix, and sharing the compute too
md: A prefix hit turns prefill into a smaller prefill with an offset: new queries see a rectangle of cached keys plus a causal triangle, at positions that continue from the cache. Hits end on block boundaries and never include the last prompt token.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: what your DNS tells the world
md: Recon results drive scope questions, not actions. Finding that `vpn.example.com` exists does not make it in scope. Check the address against the scope guard before any active step.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: From perf.data to folded stacks
md: In `perf report`, a high Children value does not mean the function is doing the work. main is 100% in every program. Sort by Self to find what executes, by Children to find which caller to change.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Visibility and durability are different events. A store becomes visible when it reaches the coherent cache, and durable only when its line reaches the persistence domain. On ADR platforms, software must close that gap explicitly.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: SPF: which servers may send for a domain
md: Misconception: "SPF pass means the sender is who they claim". SPF pass means only that the connecting IP is allowed to send for the **envelope** domain. That domain may be the attacker's own.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
md: Which end of a storage unit bit-fields start from, whether they may straddle units, and the signedness of a plain `int` bit-field are all implementation-defined in C (cppreference lists them). Two compilers or two ABIs can lay out the same bit-field struct differently, so never use bit-fields to match a wire format or a hardware register; use shifts and masks on a fixed-width integer instead.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A pose model's output is a fixed, ordered list of keypoints per person, each with a position and a confidence. Everything downstream (metrics, angles, rep counting) is arithmetic on that list.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Lattices from zero: points, bases and hard problems
md: The lattice trapdoor in one sentence: the **public key** is a pile of noisy equations, the **private key** is the secret that turns the noise back into something small, and encryption hides a message under more noise that only the key holder can strip away (next lesson, by hand).

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches
md: Pre-filtering with a flat scan is exact and its cost is proportional to the number of matches, $sn$. That makes it the best plan for restrictive filters and the worst plan for broad ones.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Bandwidth-bound code: count the bytes, skip the reads
md: Do not sprinkle streaming stores everywhere. Intel recommends them for memset-style fills larger than about half the last-level cache when the data is not read soon after. On Skylake server it warns that overusing them on smaller blocks evicts lines you need and can hit a per-core limit on non-temporal write bandwidth.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: k-anonymity: generalise and suppress until you hide in a crowd
md: k-anonymity is a property of one table against one declared set of quasi-identifiers. It says nothing about columns you forgot, other releases, or what the sensitive values in a class reveal.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy in real systems: units, trust and hazards
md: "We use differential privacy" is not a guarantee until you know three things: epsilon (and delta), the unit of privacy, and who sees the raw data. A large epsilon at event level with a trusted curator can protect very little.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Private set intersection: comparing lists without sharing them
md: Diffie-Hellman PSI works because blinded exponentiation commutes: H(x)^(ab) = H(x)^(ba). Each side blinds with a secret it never reveals, so only matching items line up. Hashing alone is not PSI, because hashes of small identifier spaces can be inverted.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 1: reading sudo rules like an auditor
md: Misconception: "NOPASSWD is the dangerous part." It does remove a hurdle for an intruder who has a shell but not the password (a web shell, a stolen SSH key). But a rule that leads to a shell is a root grant with or without a password prompt. Fix what the command can do first, then decide on the password.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: How a PRM is trained and how it scores a solution
md: A PRM is a per-step classifier read off in one forward pass. Training labels stop at the first error. To compare solutions you reduce step scores to one number; product and minimum perform similarly, but product quietly favours shorter solutions.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Generative PRMs: verifiers that reason before they judge
md: Generative PRMs phrase verification as text generation: write a step-by-step critique, then read the verdicts and a Yes probability off it. They need far fewer labels and lead on error location, at the price of many more tokens per verification and overconfident scores.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: Misconception: "more threads means more parallelism." Parallelism is capped by the number of cores. Past that, extra CPU-bound threads only take turns: they add involuntary switches, push answers later, and make threads evict each other's cache. Extra threads help only when they spend time blocked, as in the I/O scene.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
md: Every bootstrap and search optimizer trusts the metric. The DSPy docs warn that a non-deterministic metric (for example an LLM judge) makes the chosen demos "a function of metric noise as much as program quality". Make the metric deterministic where you can, validate any LLM judge against humans first, and keep a held-out set.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Why security teams script, and your first Python program
md: A script is the steps you would do by hand, written down once so they run the same way on every line. Its biggest risk is not crashing; it is quietly counting the wrong thing.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
md: Hash files in binary chunks, normalize every indicator to lowercase before comparing, and remember that a match means "known bad" while a miss means only "not this exact file".

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
md: Create the synonym set before the index that references it. Elastic's guide warns that an index pointing at a missing set becomes inoperable and must be deleted and re-created, or closed and re-opened.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Binary quantization = sign of each coordinate, compared with XOR and popcount. It buys 32x memory and very cheap comparisons, but the distance it produces is coarse and has no error guarantee.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Discounts, refunds and rewards: value that can be claimed twice
md: v2 is right for requests that arrive one at a time, and still wrong when two refunds arrive at the same instant: both can read "120 left to refund" before either is recorded, and both pay out 100. Every check of the form "read a total, decide, write" is also a race condition. Lessons 5 to 9 make it atomic.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Fixing races in the database: atomic updates, locks, constraints
md: Put the check inside the write, or lock before you read, or let a constraint say no. Then make the database refuse the bad end state too (CHECK, UNIQUE), so a race you missed fails loudly instead of paying out.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to logic and race abuse
md: Log every value-changing event with business context, alert on impossible patterns (one-time actions that succeed twice, bursts within milliseconds, flows faster than a human), and reconcile balances against ledgers. Then contain before you investigate, and retest fixes in parallel.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Indexing: how chunk size and overlap decide what can be found
md: Small chunks lose their context. D1.5 reads *or adoption. Send leave requests to the People team, who approve them.* It never says which leave. In a real handbook with ten leave policies it would match every leave question equally well. Bigger chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and spend more of the prompt.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve
md: Features used for training must be produced by the same code, against the same index state and at the same moment as the features used for serving. Log the vector at query time; do not reconstruct it later.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Trust among thieves: exit scams, takedowns and a fragmented market
md: "The group promised to delete the data" is not evidence. LockBit kept data of victims who paid (found in Operation Cronos), BlackCat cheated its own affiliate, and leaked chats from other groups named victims who had paid for silence. Plan as if stolen data will eventually be published.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: The ransom decision: negotiation, proof of life and sanctions
md: A passed proof-of-life test proves only that the actor can decrypt the files tested. Test every size class you need, especially the largest databases and virtual disks, and price the decryptor against what your surviving backups can already restore.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
md: In practice: register big pools on huge pages, keep the number of connected QPs bounded (share, or use UD for fan-out), batch posts behind one doorbell, inline small payloads, signal selectively, avoid hot atomics, and handle error completions by resetting or recreating the connection.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Treating a blank as a rating of 0 is a modelling choice, not a fact. It makes plain cosine reward items that are merely *rated by the same people*, whatever the ratings. In Sarwar et al.'s MovieLens experiments, adjusted cosine gave lower error (mean absolute error, the average size of the gap between predicted and true rating) than plain cosine or Pearson correlation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: Split by time, exclude what the user already consumed, beat tuned simple baselines, and confirm with an online experiment.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: A GROUP BY result from a HashAggregate has no defined order. If you need sorted output, write ORDER BY; do not rely on the order you happened to see.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: Misconception: reward hacking means the RL algorithm is buggy. DeepMind's analysis points the other way: the behavior comes from misspecification, and a *better* optimizer is more likely to find an intricate loophole that a weaker one would miss. Stronger RL makes the specification matter more, not less.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When the verifier is code: test hacking in coding agents
md: This grader still runs the agent's code as the same operating-system user, so that code could reach the grader's own files or leave a process running after its own ends. Production graders run the solution in a separate container or user account with no write access to the grader, keep hidden tests, and still watch transcripts (lesson 9). Isolation raises the cost of a hack; it does not prove there is none.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Putting money on risk: ALE and the FAIR model
md: ALE = SLE x ARO is the right *shape* of answer: frequency times magnitude, in money, per year. FAIR keeps that shape but estimates each factor as a range and keeps the full distribution, so you can talk about bad years, not only average ones.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: ISO/IEC 27001: an ISMS, Annex A and the certification audit
md: Check the **scope** on any certificate a vendor shows you. A certificate covering "the corporate office in Lisbon" says nothing about the SaaS product you are buying. Ask for the certificate and the SoA, or at least the scope statement, and check the issuing body is accredited.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Breach notification clocks and US disclosure rules
md: The engineering lesson from SolarWinds is about **public security statements**: trust pages, questionnaire answers, marketing claims. Every sentence like "we enforce least privilege everywhere" is a claim someone may later test against your internal tickets. Write them so they are true, keep evidence that they are, and update them when the facts change.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Accountability: what boards, CISOs and engineers have answered for
md: Breaches are survivable; cover-ups are not. Regulators judge governance: risk assessed before big changes, audit that reports independently, boards that hold management accountable, statements that match reality, and incidents disclosed on time to the people with authority to decide.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: Sync cost = bytes / bandwidth + resharding. The bytes are fixed by model size and precision; good systems avoid gathering the full model anywhere, send each rank only its shard, and keep the transfer off the critical path.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Placing GEMM, softmax and LLM decode on the roofline
md: Intensity is not fixed for a given operation. It depends on shape (thin GEMMs fall left), precision (FP8 halves the bytes per element and so doubles intensity), and how well the implementation reuses data. A naive GEMM that rereads inputs from DRAM can be memory bound even at 8192 cubed.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
md: An RRF score is not a relevance probability. Its size depends on k and on how many lists were fused (Azure AI Search notes each query contributes at most about $1/k$), so do not apply a fixed threshold to it across queries or configurations.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
md: Misconception: "Rust drivers do not need cleanup code." They need exactly as much cleanup as C drivers. The difference is that it lives once in a `Drop` impl (yours or an abstraction's) and runs on every path automatically, including early returns from `?`.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: What Rust in the kernel does not prevent, and what it costs
md: Rust in the kernel moves a large class of bugs (forgotten unlocks, unchecked errors, use-after-free through ownership mistakes) from runtime to compile time, and concentrates the rest into small, documented `unsafe` regions. It does not remove the need for review, lockdep, or testing.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: scx_simple charges `SCX_SLICE_DFL - p->scx.slice`. Its own comment warns that a task that yields has its slice zeroed and so is charged a full slice. Precise schedulers take explicit timestamps in `running` and `stopping` instead.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Safety net, failure modes and schedulers in production
md: Misconception: switching to a sched_ext scheduler is a free speedup. Each one encodes tradeoffs for a workload. scx_simple's own header says it suits a single uniform L3 and that its FIFO mode lets saturating threads drown out interactive ones. Benchmark your workload against the fair class (lesson 10 shows how), and check whether the scheduler honors the cgroup limits you rely on.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key ceremonies: the DNS root key and multi-person control
md: Multi-person control turns "trust this administrator" into "trust that M of these N people did not all collude", and a recorded ceremony turns it into something auditors and outsiders can verify.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: eval, pickle and yaml.load turn data into code
md: Ask of every parser in a diff: can this input make the parser call code? If yes (eval, pickle, unsafe YAML), the input must never come from outside the trust boundary. Pick a format that can only describe data.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Go: ignored errors, text/template and Go's review tools
md: Go review checklist: every `_` in an error position (what zero value flows on?), every shared map and variable (which lock?), every map field (who calls make?), html/template for HTML and every template.HTML conversion, and gosec, go vet, govulncheck and go test -race in CI.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Writing the finding and the fix so it gets merged
md: Do not overstate. "Critical, full compromise" on a bug that needs admin access and a rare configuration teaches developers to ignore your severities. Do not understate either: "minor input handling issue" for code execution gets it scheduled next quarter. State exactly what you proved and what you believe but did not prove.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: RADIUS and TACACS+: central logins for network devices
md: RADIUS and TACACS+ secrets are often short, reused across hundreds of devices, and left in device configuration backups. Anyone holding the secret and a packet capture can recover RADIUS passwords and forge replies. Treat the secret like a password database key: long, random, unique per device or site, and rotated.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Brewer-Nash's Chinese Wall, and choosing the right model
md: A formal model is a precise statement of what secure means for one kind of system. Pick the model by the harm you fear: disclosure, contamination, invalid change, or conflict of interest. Real systems combine several.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Segmentation and microsegmentation, planned from real traffic
md: Segmenting by host pairs is not the finish line. The billing app still talks to the domain controller; restrict that flow to the authentication ports it needs and to the app's own identity, and watch it closely.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: LLMs from zero: tokens, sampling and confident mistakes
md: Treat an LLM like a fast, fluent junior analyst who has never seen your environment, gives slightly different answers each time, sometimes invents facts, and believes whatever text it is shown.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, payload and risk
md: A vulnerability is not a risk by itself. A severe bug in software you do not run, or on a machine with no network connection, may carry very little risk. A boring weakness on an internet-facing system that attackers already scan for can carry a lot. Lesson 6 turns this into a patching order.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: EternalBlue and WannaCry: a patch, a leak and a worm
md: WannaCry: one wormable bug, a patch two months old, a leaked exploit, and organisations that had not patched or could not patch old systems. The fixes were basic: patch, remove legacy protocols, filter port 445, segment, back up.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: What a security leader is for: the CISO's job and reporting line
md: Misconception: "a higher reporting line means better security". The reporting line decides two things: whether bad news can be filtered before it reaches the people who decide, and whether the CISO is grading their own boss's work. A CISO under the CEO with no budget and no board access can be weaker than one under a CIO with a standing audit-committee slot.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Vendors and tools: buy, build, consolidate and plan the exit
md: A capability label is not a capability. "Log search" in a SIEM with a year of retention and in an XDR add-on with 30 days are different things for an investigation that looks back three months (recall dwell time in *Preparation*). Before retiring a tool: compare depth and retention, count integrations and detections built on it, check the contract's end date, and run both in parallel for a period.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Regulators and disclosure: materiality, risk factors, certifications
md: Writing "a breach could harm us" in a filing after a breach has happened is not cautious; the SEC treated it as a misleading half-truth. When a risk has materialised, say so in proportion. And never let a public statement (filing, trust page, customer questionnaire) say more than your internal records support.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Incident updates when you do not know yet
md: Never let an update outrun the evidence to sound reassuring. A confident claim that later proves wrong costs more trust than an honest "not yet known". The next lesson is a real case.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inside the search tree: selection, expansion, evaluation and backup
md: A common bug: backing up $v$ with the same sign at every level. Then the edge into a leaf is credited with the value for the player who did not choose it, and each player's search prefers moves that are good for the opponent. Store each $Q$ from the point of view of the player who made the move, and flip the sign once per ply.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Adversarial self-play for language models, and AlphaProof
md: Adversarial self-play gives an automatic curriculum, an opponent or proposer that keeps the task at the edge of ability. It does not by itself create a correct signal. The strongest results, from AlphaZero to AlphaProof, pair self-play with a judge that is never wrong.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: The server as a confused deputy
md: The server is trusted by its network, its cloud account and its own disk. Any feature that lets input choose *what the server touches* (a host, a path, a class, a lookup) lends that trust to the attacker. Defence means taking the choice away, or shrinking what the server can touch.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Path traversal and safe path joins
md: Common broken fixes: deleting `../` from the input once (nested sequences reassemble after the deletion), checking before URL-decoding (encoded dots slip through), checking the string starts with the base (`/srv/app/files-old` passes), and forgetting that on Windows the backslash `..\` works too. Normalise first, then compare whole path components.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
md: Chunked prefill trades the long prompt's time to first token for bounded step size: lower peak activation memory (activations are the intermediate tensors a forward pass keeps, and they grow with the number of tokens in the pass) and, when decodes are mixed in, steadier token gaps for everyone else. It does not reduce total prefill work.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
md: CH trades a one-time preprocessing pass (contract nodes, add shortcuts) for tiny queries: two upward searches that meet at the most important node of the route, then shortcuts are unpacked back into original roads.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
md: Misconception: "wider vectors always mean proportionally faster code." Width is only the upper bound. Memory bandwidth, latency chains and loop overheads decide how much of it you actually get.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Why a general-purpose heap wastes memory
md: Allocators are not just faster or slower `malloc`s. Each design gives up a freedom (free in any order, any size, any type) and gets speed or lower fragmentation in return. Ask which freedom your workload can give up.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: "Disaggregated" here is about trainer versus rollout GPUs. It is unrelated to PD (prefill-decode) disaggregation (`--prefill-num-servers`), which puts SGLang's prefill (processing the whole prompt in one pass) and decode (generating one token at a time) on different servers, and it does not imply async training by itself.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
md: Async in slime means: same train.py, different rollout function, separate GPU pools. You trade a bounded amount of policy staleness for not waiting on the slowest trajectory.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Ethereum accounts, transactions and gas
md: Gas is also a security limit. Each block has a gas cap, so a function whose work grows with user-controlled data (a loop over every depositor) can become impossible to call. The Solidity docs warn this "can cause the complete contract to be stalled". Lesson 9 shows the fix.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Upgradeable proxies and storage collisions
md: In a proxy system, storage layout is part of the interface. Any write to the slot that holds the implementation address is an upgrade, whoever makes it. Detect: watch that slot's value every block, not just `Upgraded` events (Bybit's slot-0 overwrite emitted none), and run OpenZeppelin's upgrade-safety checks before each upgrade. Respond: a timelock leaves time to cancel a bad upgrade or let users exit.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When the attacker calls the help desk: MFA resets and new devices
md: The help desk is part of your attack surface and part of your sensor network. Alert on MFA resets and new device enrollments for privileged users, correlate them with what happens next, and verify with the real person through a channel the caller cannot control. Okta also recommends stronger help desk identity checks, such as visual verification.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Security is a secondary task: why people work around it
md: Misconception: "people ignore security because they do not care". Adams and Sasse found people inventing their own schemes to comply, and Herley shows that ignoring costly advice is often the rational choice. When most people bypass a control, treat it as a design defect in the control.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Physical security in layers: zones, CPTED and access rules
md: Misconception: "physical security is the facilities team's job". Many intrusion paths end at a network port or an unlocked laptop. Security engineers should own the requirements (which zones protect which systems, what gets logged, how alerts reach the SOC) together with facilities.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
md: L1 penalises size, so it shrinks every active latent. TopK (fixed k), Gated (separate gate) and JumpReLU (learned per-latent thresholds with an L0 penalty) all separate deciding which latents fire from estimating how big they are.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Where SAEs fall short: absorption, missing features and weak baselines
md: Sparsity rewards absorbing a parent feature into its children, so SAE latents can have silent holes. Matryoshka and BatchTopK reduce the damage, but SAEs are not canonical units, and on labelled tasks simple baselines such as difference-in-means and linear probes usually match or beat them.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
md: Kriging weights come from solving a linear system, not from a fixed formula. That lets them account for redundancy between sensors (declustering) and for sensors hidden behind others (screening), and it yields an error variance for every estimate.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect
md: Speedup is not tokens per pass. A draft that is accurate but slow (high alpha, high c) can lose to a weaker but nearly free one. Leviathan et al. found drafts about two orders of magnitude smaller than the target usually balanced alpha and c best.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
md: Whisper is an audio-conditioned language model. The encoder turns 30 s of log-mel into 1500 vectors; the decoder generates the transcript token by token, with language, task and timestamps expressed as tokens in the same sequence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: Stack memory lives exactly as long as the function call that created it. Allocation and release are a pointer adjustment, which is why the size must be bounded and why anything that must outlive the call has to go somewhere else: the heap.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: TLB reach = entries x page size. Working sets beyond it pay a page walk on most random accesses; huge pages raise reach by 512 times, and every unmap in a multithreaded process may interrupt other CPUs.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Lab: build, sweep and evaluate a steering vector on a small chat model
md: Three things bite first attempts. The chat template inserts a default system prompt ("You are Qwen...") when you give none. Qwen's tokenizer turns "(A" into a single token, so the answer letter is not a separate position: read activations at the "(A" token and score the "(A" and "(B" tokens. And the hook must cope with both output types of a decoder layer. Print the tokens of one full prompt before anything else.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Watermark = the processor's estimate of how far event time has progressed. It decides when a window first fires; allowed lateness decides how long the window can still be corrected; anything beyond is dropped or side-output. Every choice trades latency for completeness.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, teacher forcing and cross-attention
md: A causal mask sets the scores of future positions to minus infinity before softmax, so with teacher forcing every target position trains in one pass without seeing its own answer. Cross-attention is the same function with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: "Transformer" does not mean "GPT" (generative pre-trained transformer, OpenAI's line of decoder-only language models). The 2017 model is an encoder-decoder for translation. Decoder-only language models keep only its masked self-attention stack; encoder-only models keep only the unmasked encoder.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Tuning k1 and b on a real test collection
md: Never tune on the queries you report. Use a dev split or cross-validation, and treat a flat surface as a sign that the defaults are fine: a 0.002 dev gain over the default is within noise for a few hundred queries.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
md: A GPT is just: embed (token + position), $L$ x [pre-LN causal attention, pre-LN MLP, each added to the residual stream], final LayerNorm, project back to vocabulary scores with the tied embedding matrix.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
md: A common slip is evaluating the outer derivative at $x$ instead of at the inner value. Here $f'(u) = 2u$ must use $u = 7$, giving 14, not $2 \times 2 = 4$. That is why the forward values are computed and stored first: the backward step needs them.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: A rising loss does not always mean a bug in your gradients. With a correct gradient, too large a learning rate alone makes training diverge, as $\eta = 0.35$ did here. Lowering $\eta$ is the first thing to try.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
md: Do not test your quoting in zsh and assume bash agrees. zsh, the default interactive shell on macOS, does **not** word-split unquoted parameter expansions unless the `SH_WORD_SPLIT` option is set. Scripts that start with `#!/bin/bash` or `#!/bin/sh` (a first line naming the interpreter, the shebang of lesson 4) follow the splitting rules shown here.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: `set -e` is a safety net, not error handling. It misses failures inside functions called from conditions and in `&&` chains. For steps that matter, check explicitly: `if ! cp src dst; then echo 'copy failed' >&2; exit 1; fi`.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
md: Skip-gram is not trained to be a good language model; the prediction task is a pretext. Mikolov et al. say plainly that the skip-gram model is only concerned with learning high-quality vector representations. After training, the output layer is usually thrown away and the input vectors are kept as the embeddings.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
md: A GPU is a throughput machine. It hides slow memory by keeping many warps in flight, not by making any single access fast. Give it too little parallel work and the SMs sit idle.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
md: KV cache size = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes, per token, per sequence. It grows linearly with context and with batch size, and it is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: Misconception: "the compiler makes something the CPU runs straight off the disk." The CPU only fetches instructions from memory. An executable is inert until the OS loader maps it into a process's memory and points the CPU at its entry point.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: Never return a pointer to a local variable. Its stack slot is reused by the very next call (as the second call to square reused the first one's slot), so the pointer soon points at unrelated data. Use the heap (malloc) for data that must outlive the function.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
md: A low pretraining loss does not mean a helpful model. The loss rewards matching the *distribution* of internet text, including its errors, rudeness and rambling. That is exactly why the later stages exist.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Where preference data comes from: guidelines, safety, AI feedback
md: Preference data is a design choice: who labels, under which guidelines, on which prompts, with which ratings. Separate signals (helpfulness and safety) and AI labels from written principles (RLAIF) are now standard ingredients of post-training.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
md: Skip pointers only help AND-style intersections, where we look for a specific docID. For OR we must output every posting of both lists anyway, so there is nothing to skip. Skips are also costly to maintain when postings lists change often.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Getting the top k fast: tiers, MaxScore and WAND
md: Safe top-k pruning keeps a running threshold, the k-th best score so far, and a score upper bound per term (or per block). Any document whose bounds cannot beat the threshold is skipped with the skip data, so the top k is exactly what exhaustive scoring would return.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Multi-file C: headers, include guards, static, extern and make
md: Headers hold declarations (`extern` variables, prototypes) behind an include guard; exactly one .c file holds each definition; `static` keeps helpers private. A Makefile lists what each file depends on, and make rebuilds only what is older than its inputs.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Before you keep a pointer, ask how long the object behind it lives. Locals die when their function returns, malloc'd memory dies at free, and realloc can retire the old address at any call.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
md: Develop C with `-Wall -Wextra -g -fsanitize=address,undefined` on, and fix every warning. Most of the pointer and lifetime bugs from this course then fail loudly at the exact line instead of corrupting memory silently.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: Shared XOR mutable: any number of `&T`, or exactly one `&mut T`, never both at the same point in the program. A borrow is live from creation to last use.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell
md: Default to borrowing; move when the callee should keep the value; clone when copies are cheap or necessary; use `Rc`/`RefCell` only for data with genuinely shared ownership.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: $A\mathbf{x}$ is both a stack of dot products (one per row) and a weighted sum of columns. The columns of $A$ are the images of the basis vectors, so they fully describe the map.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Tensors, batches and broadcasting: shapes in real code
md: Broadcasting checks sizes, never meaning. A loss computed from (3, 1) predictions and (3,) targets averages 9 differences instead of 3 and raises nothing. Assert shapes where arrays from different places meet: `assert pred.shape == y.shape`.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Many features: linear regression in matrix form and feature scaling
md: With many features, predictions are $\hat y = Xw$ and the MSE gradient is $\frac{2}{n}X^\top(Xw - y)$. Its minimum solves the normal equations $X^\top Xw = X^\top y$. Features on very different scales stretch the bowl, so gradient descent crawls; standardizing them rounds it out.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Validation and penalties: choosing lambda, L2 and L1
md: Choose capacity and penalty strength by **validation** error and keep the test set for one final check. L2 (weight decay) shrinks every weight a little each step; L1 pins weak weights at exactly zero and so selects features.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Why a single linear layer cannot learn XOR
md: Misconception: a deeper network of linear layers is more expressive. It is not; it is exactly as expressive as one linear layer. Another one: universal approximation means any network will learn any function. It only guarantees that suitable weights exist.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradients through depth: vanishing, exploding and unlucky seeds
md: Backprop computes the exact gradient of the loss at the current weights; it does not guarantee a good solution. The loss surface of a network is not **convex** (bowl-shaped, so that every valley is the lowest one), so the starting point matters. Lesson: always check the loss curve, and try more than one seed.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement
md: Memory is a cache for pages, and a disk-backed miss costs about 100,000 memory accesses. A replacement policy tries to approximate OPT using the past: LRU in principle, the use bit and the clock algorithm in practice, preferring clean pages.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: how a hard disk spends its time
md: A random disk I/O is almost all positioning: seek plus half a rotation, milliseconds, against microseconds of transfer. Make requests large and sequential, and let the scheduler order them by position.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Conditioning means restricting attention to the outcomes consistent with what you know, then renormalizing so they sum to 1. Almost every formula in this course is that one idea applied carefully.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Covariance, correlation and the multivariate Gaussian
md: Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and sunburns are correlated because sunny weather drives both: a **confounder**, a third variable that causes both. The Deep Learning textbook by Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville makes the same point about conditioning: P(from Germany | speaks German) is high, but teaching someone German does not change where they are from.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Power and sample size: planning an A/B test before running it
md: Power depends on the effect size you assume. Choose the smallest effect worth acting on before you see data, not the effect you hope for and not the effect a finished test happened to show.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
md: A scaling study is an experiment design problem: budgets spread over orders of magnitude, sizes that bracket each valley, a properly ended schedule per run, then two fits (IsoFLOP parabolas and the parametric form) that should agree, each with bootstrap error bars.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
md: nDCG@k answers: what fraction of the best achievable discounted gain did the top k results capture? It is the default when labels are graded and users look mostly at the first page.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
md: Each stage covers another's blind spot: BM25 for rare exact terms, the bi-encoder for meaning across different words, the cross-encoder for precise final ordering on a short list. Evaluate the whole pipeline on your own queries with a metric such as recall at k (the share of relevant passages that appear in the top k results).

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Build a byte-level BPE tokenizer in Python
md: Decode with `errors="replace"` (or keep bytes) whenever ids can be cut at arbitrary points: one token at a time while streaming, or a sequence the model generated that may not be valid UTF-8. With strict decoding a partial character raises an error. When streaming, keep the bytes and only show the characters once all their bytes have arrived.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Residual connections: why 56 layers trained worse than 20
md: A residual block computes $x + F(x)$. The identity path makes doing nothing easy to learn and gives the gradient a direct route to every layer. Start each branch near zero so that a deep stack begins as one identity map rather than a variance amplifier.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude fewer distance computations. Every ANN number you read (or report) should come as a pair: recall@k and speed, measured against exact brute-force results on the same queries.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Version ranges and lockfiles: why new code arrives unasked
md: A lockfile only protects installs that use it. A Dockerfile that copies only package.json, `npx some-tool`, a global install, or a developer running `npm update` all resolve ranges fresh. The axios post-mortem told users who were "pinned to a clean version" and ran no fresh install in the window that they were fine.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: xz-utils I: two years of patient social engineering
md: The xz attack was a trust attack, not a technical exploit of git, signing or builds. Every step was done by a legitimate maintainer with legitimate rights. Defences are partly social: fund and share maintenance of critical projects, add second reviewers for releases, and treat sudden pressure to hand over control or upgrade fast as a warning sign.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
md: Synthetic data are useful when an outside signal decides what is kept, diversity is designed in, and real data stay in the training mix. Model collapse is what happens when all three are missing.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR
md: Every `read` and `write` may block, move fewer bytes than asked, or fail with `EINTR` or `EAGAIN`. Loop until all bytes are moved, retry on `EINTR`, and treat `EAGAIN` as "wait until the descriptor is ready".

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp
md: strace shows which calls a program makes and how often; getrusage shows the page faults that strace cannot see; seccomp turns a list of needed calls into an enforced allow-list. All three work on syscall numbers and miss the vDSO.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: How a mobile network fits together: radio, core and the HLR
md: The home HLR/HSS holds each subscriber's secret key and current location, and other networks must be able to query it for roaming to work. Mobile security is largely about who is allowed to ask it what.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: SIM and eSIM: the key in your pocket, and how it gets there
md: The SIM is a computer that holds the subscriber's key and runs code. Protect what can reach it (filter OTA and binary SMS) and treat every way of putting a number onto a new card or eSIM as a credential reset.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Detecting GNSS spoofing, and authenticated navigation signals
md: Spoofing is caught by inconsistency: with physics, with your own clock's history, with other receivers and other time sources. Signing the navigation data (OSNMA) raises the bar, and a backup timing source keeps you running while you investigate.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
md: Test-time scaling has two halves that can fail independently. **Coverage**: does any attempt contain a correct answer? **Precision**: can you pick it out? The next two lessons take them one at a time.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Tree search for reasoning: Tree of Thoughts, MCTS, inference laws
md: Tree search pays when you have a step-level evaluator you can trust (code that runs, a checked answer, a strong PRM) and when early mistakes are expensive, as in Game of 24. With a weak evaluator, more search mostly finds the evaluator's mistakes, the over-optimization seen in lesson 5. And always compare at equal compute: rollouts are not free.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: One gradient step on a key-value loss is the delta rule
md: One step of online gradient descent (one gradient step per token, in arrival order) on the regression loss is exactly the DeltaNet update with $\beta = \eta$. The TTT paper says so directly: DeltaNet is TTT-Linear with mini-batch size 1, minus the LayerNorm and residual. TTT is the framework; the delta rule is its simplest instance.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
md: Per-CPU does not automatically mean scalable. The paper found that padding and aligning each CPU's structure to its own cache line was critical for linear scaling. Without it, the per-CPU counters of neighbouring CPUs share a line and you are back to cache line ping-pong through false sharing.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: An intelligence-driven hunt: living off the land and Volt Typhoon
md: LOTL hunts are baseline hunts in disguise. The tools are legitimate, so the evidence is never the tool alone: it is the tool used by an account, on a host, at a time, or in a sequence that this environment has not seen before.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Grading sources and information: the Admiralty code
